title: More and More Global Leaders Went to Chinese Colleges. Does That Matter?
text:
More and More Global Leaders Went to Chinese Colleges. Does That Matter?

The Diplomat

WANG Zhao/AFP/Getty Images

The following excerpt is from an op-ed published in The Diplomat on August 29, 2026, written by Kevin Zongzhe Li, a Fellow at ASPI"s Center for China Analysis. On June 23, 2026, South Korean Prime Minister Kim Min-seok walked onto the campus of Tsinghua University in Beijing, where he had earned a law degree in 2010. “I believe that my time studying at Tsinghua University will remain one of the most beautiful memories of my life, forever cherished and held close to my heart,” he told his hosts. Kim had flown in from Seoul on early morning flights, he recalled, just to make it to class on time. (Kim has since resigned from office to become the chair of the ruling Democratic Party.)Three weeks earlier, Lao President Thongloun Sisoulith had stood in the dormitory room at the Central Party School where he had lived during a month-long program in 2000. “Though the campus has undergone some changes,” he said, “the places where I lived and studied remain just the same.” Both leaders returned to a Beijing alma mater within three weeks of each other. They are not alone. Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, the president of Kazakhstan, studied at the Beijing Linguistic Institute (now known as the Beijing Language and Culture University) in 1983-84 and speaks fluent Mandarin. In April 2026, Le Minh Hung took office as Vietnam’s prime minister; in 1996, he had completed a training course on market economy and financial analysis at Shanghai University of Finance and Economics. With four neighborhood countries now having top leaders who have studied in China, does this mark a new phase in Chinese educational diplomacy in its periphery, or is it little more than a biographical curiosity?Read the full op-ed here.
